scope: US-headquartered humanoid builders plus foreign companies with substantial US humanoid operations and adjacent US embodied-AI platform companies.
funding_methodology: Funding observations are the latest major disclosed raise or transaction capital, not necessarily cumulative capital raised. Read each source card before comparing companies.
valuation_methodology: Values are dated observations, not live appraisals. Private marks use the latest completed disclosed financing when available; proposed transactions and reported talks are labeled separately. Tesla is shown at whole-company public market capitalization, not an Optimus segment valuation. Boston Dynamics uses its 2020 acquisition basis because no current standalone mark is public. Undisclosed is more accurate than an inferred number.
evolution_thesis: Fact: capital, embodied-AI talent, and startup formation remain concentrated in the Bay Area, while Boston and Pittsburgh retain unusually deep robotics institutions and Austin, Oregon, and Southern California anchor major hardware programs. Projection: over the next 3–5 years, model development is likely to remain concentrated near AI talent and capital, while fleet operations, integration, manufacturing, and field-service hiring spread toward customer and industrial corridors. Commercial evidence—not demo capability—should determine whether humanoid-specific firms sustain their current valuation premium.

companies.valuation_note: Figure's official Series C announcement states more than $1B raised at a $39B post-money valuation. This is the latest disclosed financing mark, not a live valuation.

hubs.name: Bay Area
hubs.thesis: The densest overlap of frontier-AI researchers, venture capital, semiconductor infrastructure, startup mobility, and robotics software formation.
hubs.outlook: Likely to retain model, data, and executive concentration; high costs may push hardware production and fleet operations elsewhere.

hubs.name: Boston / Cambridge
hubs.thesis: Long-duration robotics depth across dynamics, manipulation, autonomy, biotech, and industrial systems, supported by dense research institutions.
hubs.outlook: Should remain a durable hardware and industrial-robotics cluster even if humanoid venture formation is more visible in California.

hubs.name: Pittsburgh
hubs.thesis: CMU creates unusually concentrated talent in robot learning, autonomy, field robotics, perception, and safety.
hubs.outlook: Likely to remain a talent and research engine; scaling firms may add Bay Area capital-facing offices while retaining Pittsburgh technical teams.

hubs.name: Austin
hubs.thesis: University robotics, Tesla manufacturing, semiconductor depth, lower operating costs, and Texas industrial customers reinforce a hardware-to-deployment corridor.
hubs.outlook: Well positioned for humanoid manufacturing, validation, and customer deployment roles, not only research.

hubs.name: Pacific Northwest
hubs.thesis: Oregon State's legged-robotics lineage anchors Agility, while Seattle contributes cloud, logistics, and manipulation demand through Amazon and a strong software workforce.
hubs.outlook: Oregon can become a meaningful humanoid manufacturing node; Seattle remains strong in logistics autonomy and cloud-connected fleets.

hubs.name: Southern California
hubs.thesis: Aerospace, defense, entertainment, logistics, and university labs support robotics that must work in complex real-world environments.
hubs.outlook: Defense and aerospace demand may pull embodied-AI talent toward rugged autonomy and manufacturing rather than consumer humanoids.

hubs.name: Texas industrial corridor
hubs.thesis: Houston offers direct access to shipbuilding, energy, space, heavy industry, and field-service problems that reward rugged robots over polished demos.
hubs.outlook: Could become a proving ground for hazardous-work humanoids and industrial service, with fewer foundation-model headquarters than the Bay Area.
